title: Townhome CMA with Craig - May 13, 2026
summary: Craig walks agent Jake through a live CMA for a townhome listing in Lehi, Utah (Innocenti Days / Leather Ridge community). Covers townhome-specific comp selection tricks, adjusting for garage size (one vs two car), end unit vs mid unit premiums, finished vs unfinished basement impact, rear-loaded vs front-loaded layout preferences, private yard value, and the critical 'gut check' step of analyzing active competition before setting list price. Recommends pricing at $450K with marketing strategies for a buyer's market.

broker_guidance.scenario: Doing a townhome CMA and comps seem scarce
broker_guidance.guidance: Remove 'townhouse' filter from the search. Sometimes townhomes are mislisted as single family or other types. Focus on geography first, then refine by square footage and other criteria. Also expand year built range — townhome communities are usually built within 1-2 years but the Great Recession delayed some developments.

broker_guidance.scenario: Subject property has a two-car garage but comps have one-car garages
broker_guidance.guidance: One-car garage vs two-car garage can kill townhome value by $30-40K. Craig has been doing deep dive research on this for his own townhome builds in Riverton. Be conservative but realistic — he used a $15-20K adjustment in this analysis, though he suspects the true impact may be higher.
broker_guidance.client_language: The one-car garage feature has been a deal killer for townhome values in my research.

broker_guidance.scenario: Subject property is a mid-unit vs end-unit comps
broker_guidance.guidance: End units carry a premium. Craig has seen appraisers give $5-15K for end unit status. In this analysis he used $10K as a conservative adjustment. Always verify whether comps are end or mid units and adjust accordingly.
broker_guidance.client_language: On townhomes I like to make an adjustment for mid versus end unit.

broker_guidance.scenario: Subject property has an unfinished basement but comps have finished basements
broker_guidance.guidance: Unfinished basement is one of the biggest value hits. In this analysis, the unfinished basement was the primary reason the automated valuation came in lower. Finished basement adds significant value — always verify basement finish percentage in the tax records and adjust accordingly.
broker_guidance.client_language: That's where you are getting the biggest hit — the subject property's basement is unfinished.

broker_guidance.guidance: Rear-loaded (alley-loaded) townhomes are less desirable than front-loaded because buyers lose the private backyard. Front-loaded units often have a small grassy yard even with a one-car garage. Craig considers rear-loaded layouts a 'detrimental floor plan' for subdivision layout. Adjust down for rear-loaded if comps are front-loaded with private yards.
broker_guidance.client_language: Cities are in love with these rear-loaded townhomes and I just am not. There is some value in having a private backyard.

broker_guidance.scenario: Setting list price in a buyer's market
broker_guidance.guidance: Do the 'gut check' — search active competition in the price range and area to see what buyers' alternatives are. In this case, there was virtually no competition under $480K for 2000+ sq ft townhomes. This supported pricing aggressively at $450K. Craig recommended nothing higher than $470K, with $450K being the sweet spot for attention.
broker_guidance.client_language: If you're at four fifty, you are going to have a lot of attention on this. I would recommend nothing higher than four seventy.

broker_guidance.scenario: Seller wants to include washer/dryer or appliances
broker_guidance.guidance: In a buyer's market, including appliances can be a small advantage. In a seller's market, don't mention them upfront — use them as a negotiating chip during repair negotiations. Either exclude them from the listing and offer them instead of repairs, or include them upfront for attention in a buyer's market.
broker_guidance.client_language: You don't mention it as being included and then wait for them to offer. At that point, it becomes a negotiating chip.

broker_guidance.scenario: Tenants in place and seller wants to delay showings/photos
broker_guidance.guidance: Use 'Coming Soon' status. It gets the listing in front of people without counting days on market. You only need 2 pictures officially. Must go active within 21 days. Promote heavily on social media during coming soon period to build anticipation.
broker_guidance.client_language: Coming soon status is available. Should we use it? Absolutely because it gets in front of people.

broker_guidance.scenario: Seller wants to price higher and offer concessions
broker_guidance.guidance: $460K with $10K seller concessions can work, or price at $470-480K with a rate buydown advertised prominently. Craig suggests calculating the cost of a 2-1 buydown and advertising 'initial rate X%'' on the opening graphic. This can generate traction at higher price points in a buyer's market.
broker_guidance.client_language: You could do four sixty and advertise photos saying ten thousand seller concessions. Or call and say how much would it cost for a two one rate buy down and advertise that.

broker_guidance.scenario: Hardwood floors or upgrades — do they add value?
broker_guidance.guidance: Only adjust for upgrades if the comps DON'T have similar quality. In this analysis, all comps had good flooring (different types but all good), so no adjustment was made for the subject's scraped hardwood. Wood as a 'luxury floor' doesn't carry the same premium in Lehi as it would in Alpine or Park City.
broker_guidance.client_language: All comps had good flooring. Different kinds, but all had good flooring, so nothing that would be more advantage.

broker_guidance.scenario: One comp sold for significantly more than the others
broker_guidance.guidance: When one comp is an anomaly, investigate why. In this case, a $479K sale in the same community outperformed the market despite having no special features beyond a private yard. It sold in 2.5 weeks during a slower time with low turnover — likely due to scarcity. Don't let one outlier skew your analysis; weight the majority of comps more heavily.
broker_guidance.client_language: This dude outperformed the market. These others is where I am seeing it come in at.

broker_guidance.scenario: Verifying MLS data accuracy before using a comp
broker_guidance.guidance: Always cross-check MLS input data against tax records. Craig verified square footage, year built, lot size, and PUD vs condo status by checking Utah County appraisal info. Kudos the listing agent when data is input correctly — bad data makes for bad CMAs.
broker_guidance.client_language: We can confidently take this MLS number and use its data because this was input really, really well.

steps: Verify MLS data against tax records (square footage, year built, lot size, PUD vs condo)
Remove 'townhouse' filter when searching comps — properties may be mislisted
Expand year built range if needed (communities sometimes built over several years)
Adjust for garage size — one-car vs two-car can be a $30-40K value difference
Adjust for end unit vs mid unit premium ($5-15K)
Adjust for finished vs unfinished basement — one of the biggest value impacts
Adjust for rear-loaded vs front-loaded layout — rear-loaded is less desirable
Adjust for private yard vs no private yard — especially important for pet owners
Do the 'gut check' — search active competition in the price range and geography
Price aggressively in a buyer's market; nothing higher than $470K for this property
Consider seller concessions or rate buydown advertising instead of higher list price
Use 'Coming Soon' status to build buzz without counting DOM when tenants delay access
Promote coming soon listings on social media
Don't adjust for upgrades if all comps have similar quality levels

objections.objection: Seller wants to price at $480K or higher
objections.response: You'll likely sit on the market. There are a lot of unmotivated buyers in the $470s. At $450K you'll get a ton of attention and likely outperform the comps anyway. If they insist on $480K, advertise a rate buydown prominently.

objections.objection: Seller thinks their upgrades justify a higher price
objections.response: Only if the comps DON'T have similar upgrades. In this case, all comps had good flooring and kitchens. The scraped hardwood doesn't add value when every comp also has quality flooring. Wood floors are not a luxury differentiator in this market like they are in Alpine or Park City.

objections.objection: Tenants won't allow showings or photos yet
objections.response: Use Coming Soon status. You only need 2 pictures, it doesn't count days on market, and you have 21 days to go active. Promote on socials during the coming soon period to build anticipation.

objections.objection: There are no recent comps in the community
objections.response: Expand search geography to adjacent communities with similar product. Check if new construction nearby (like DR Horton) will affect pricing. Also expand the sold date range — Craig went back 180 days when needed. Look at rambler-style townhomes as additional data points even if not identical.

objections.objection: Seller wants to include washer/dryer in the listing
objections.response: In a buyer's market, including them can be a small advantage. But consider excluding them and using them as a chip during repair negotiations. If buyer asks for repairs, counter with 'just take the washer/dryer instead.'

confidence_notes: All chunk texts are direct excerpts from the transcript with line numbers verified against the raw transcript file. Speaker 1 is Craig (broker/trainer). Speaker 2 is Jake (agent). Craig performed a live CMA using the MLS system during the call. Property address was Innocenti Days in Lehi, Utah (Leather Ridge community). Craig's pricing recommendation was $450K with a ceiling of $470K. The CMA included 5 initial comps from the community plus additional comps from adjacent communities when expanded to 180 days. Craig is actively building townhomes in Riverton and shared his research on garage size impact.
